title: What role for cultural heritage institutions in the age of AI?
content:
Three recent initiatives address the role of the cultural heritage sector amid the rise of AI:

  • the European Commission’s call for evidence on the AI Strategy for the Cultural and Creative Sectors;
  • A European Parliament own-initiative report on the cultural and creative sectors in the age of AI; and
  • the policy paper entitled Beyond adopter and supplier: putting cultural heritage at the heart of Europe’s Public by the European Heritage Hub, an EU-funded project bringing together stakeholders from the cultural heritage sector.

    • All three initiatives rightly recognise the dual role of cultural heritage institutions as users of AI systems and providers of resources for AI development. They also raise valid concerns about the visibility and discoverability of Europe’s diverse cultural heritage and less-resourced languages. Yet only the European Heritage Hub’s policy paper and a handful of the 5,442 contributions to the call for evidence envision cultural heritage and other knowledge institutions as active participants in shaping a future with AI.

title: Video recording of COMMUNIA Salon: Time to fix copyright
content:
The EU Commission is proposing to reopen copyright but its scope is far too narrow! Last week, we hosted a salon where we offered our first take on the public consultation, analysing what the Commission has in mind for its new copyright initiative, and crucially, where the blind spots are.

In its current state, the consultation desperately tries to reconcile the interests of AI developers to innovate and rightholders to get remunerated, mainly by emphasizing the importance of transparency and highlighting the value of licensing.

title: Preliminary response to the consultation for a better copyright environment
content:
Today, COMMUNIA releases its preliminary response to the targeted consultation on a potential initiative for a better copyright environment for European creativity and innovation (available for download in .docx and .pdf format).1 The consultation addresses important concerns around copyright and generative AI as well as the research framework, but has some important blind spots. Stakeholders should take note of the 10 November 2026 deadline (updated) for making their own submissions.

The Commission is considering targeted changes to the EU’s copyright framework to enhance the resilience and competitiveness of Europe’s cultural and creative sectors and to promote research and innovation. After having conducted an open-format call for evidence before the summer break, the European Commission is now asking stakeholders to contribute to a structured consultation.

title: 5 Fixes to Copyright
content:
Today, COMMUNIA is launching fivefixes.eu, a new campaign website setting out five targeted changes to EU copyright law that could deliver significant benefits for research and innovation in Europe.

Policymakers must address five persistent problems that prevent Europe’s knowledge ecosystem from reaching its full potential. With the public consultation on a potential initiative for a better copyright environment for European creativity and innovation now underway, our campaign highlights practical solutions to these barriers.

A competitive European economy depends on access to high-quality knowledge resources and legal certainty for those who use them. Today, restrictive copyright rules and unfair licensing practices too often stand in the way. Our campaign focuses on five issues:

  • Barriers to sharing research data: Researchers face restrictions on sharing data with collaborators or for purposes of validation.
  • Obstacles to open access: Researchers cannot always make their publications openly available, even when their work is publicly funded.
  • Unfair licensing terms: Knowledge institutions face contracts that arbitrarily restrict how digital resources can be used.

title: COMMUNIA Salon: Time to fix copyright
content:
The Commission has put copyright back on the menu. This is a chance to remove longstanding issues, but will the initiative address all of them?

Join COMMUNIA on Wednesday, 7 October, at 15:00 CEST for a special online salon to explore that question. We will share our first assessment of the recently opened public consultation and discuss the changes needed to support research, public-interest AI and the knowledge institutions on which both depend.

Building on the call for evidence before the summer break, the consultation addresses four areas: copyright and generative AI; online piracy of time-sensitive copyright-protected content; the use in the EU of sound recordings by nationals of non-EU countries; and copyright and research. The salon will concentrate on generative AI and research, where reform could make a significant difference to how knowledge is accessed, shared and used.

title: Meeting with Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation Ekaterina Zaharieva
content:
Last week, COMMUNIA joined IFLA, LIBER and SPARC Europe for a meeting with Ekaterina Zaharieva, Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation, to discuss the upcoming European Research Area (ERA) Act.

During this constructive exchange, we highlighted two priorities: an EU-wide secondary publication right to make publicly funded research openly available, and a general scientific research exception to create a harmonised copyright framework that enables researchers across Europe to use and build on copyright-protected research materials.

As we have argued  since the beginning of this mandate, Europe must remove persistent barriers that prevent libraries and other knowledge institutions from fulfilling their public mission, particularly in the digital environment. The ERA Act offers an important opportunity to address these barriers and help turn the “Fifth Freedom”—the free movement of researchers, knowledge and technology across the EU—into a reality.

We thank Commissioner Zaharieva and her cabinet for welcoming us and engaging with our proposals. We look forward to the Commission’s proposal for the ERA Act and to continuing this dialogue as the legislation takes shape.

title: Extending the Digital Fairness Act to the knowledge economy
content:
With the Digital Fairness Act (DFA) the Commission aims to address a number of pressing issues faced by consumers and businesses in the digital environment. This includes dark patterns, addictive design, unfair personalisation and pricing practices as well as unfair digital contracts.

In the digital environment, consumers often face situations that are not designed to be in their best interest, but rather to extract their money or time. As a result, the discussions around the DFA are already shaping up to focus on a few hot topics such as dark patterns, addictive design and protection of minors. However, the DFA also presents a great opportunity to strengthen access to knowledge and culture in Europe, and to remedy some of the failings of the digital licensing market.

title: Our response to the Commission’s call for evidence on the AI Strategy for the Cultural and Creative Sectors
content:
The European Commission concluded a call for evidence on its AI Strategy for the Cultural and Creative Sectors. Last week, COMMUNIA submitted its response (full text available as a PDF), highlighting two priorities: enabling the development of public-interest AI and safeguarding the public information ecosystem on which AI systems depend.

The strategy complements the Commission’s recently concluded call for evidence on a better copyright environment for European creativity and innovation (see our response). While some of the barriers we identify require legislative reform, the strategy can establish a broader vision for promoting access to culture, knowledge and information in the age of AI.

The cultural and creative sectors can support AI development by providing access to high-quality data. Yet several barriers prevent research and cultural heritage institutions from realising this potential:

  • National cultural heritage laws can restrict the reuse of works and artefacts that are already in the Public Domain.
  • Exclusive digitisation agreements keep around two million digitised Public Domain books from being made broadly available.
  • Paywalls restrict access to publicly funded research.

title: COMMUNIA Salon: The Rodin Case
content:
On 13 October, 14:00 to 15:00 CEST, join us for a new COMMUNIA Salon exploring the French “Rodin case” and a deceptively simple question at the heart of access to cultural heritage: Should 3D scans of works in the Public Domain be freely available for reuse, including for commercial purposes?

The dispute at hand, the so-called “Rodin Case”, started in 2018, when American artist Cosmo Wenman requested access to 3D scans of several sculptures by Auguste Rodin held by the Musée Rodin. France’s Commission for Access to Administrative Documents (CADA) backed his request, but the museum refused to release the files. In 2023, the Administrative Court of Paris piled on more pressure, ordering the museum to provide access.

However, instead of putting this dispute to bed once and for all, the case then made its way to the Council of State which,  in December 2025, reversed course. Unlike previous instances, it ruled that the collections of cultural heritage institutions do not constitute administrative documents and that the Musée Rodin was therefore not required to provide access to the scans.

title: Digital Omnibus: MEPs want to save the open government data framework
content:
During the summer, the Digital Omnibus (aka Data Omnibus) saw some welcome developments in the European Parliament. Members of the European Parliament tabled amendments both to the joint LIBE/ITRE draft report and to the JURI’s draft opinion, targeting the legal provisions we are most concerned about: Articles 32k(3) and 32r(4).

The Data Omnibus is a contentious file due to the proposed changes to the EU data protection regime. More than 1800 amendments were tabled in the main Committees alone. Therefore, we were pleased to see the (less debated) proposals concerning exclusive digitisation arrangements and open licenses not being neglected. In this blogpost, we analyse the amendments related to those provisions, and assess how they address COMMUNIA’s concerns.
